KEY MESSAGE 1...Dry today with seasonably cool temperatures.

High pressure settles in over the region today along with a notably 
drier airmass. Initially breezy conditions early this morning will 
wane heading into the late morning/early afternoon. A cooler, more 
seasonable airmass moves overhead today, dropping 925 mb 
temperatures from the 16-18C range to generally just below 10C. This 
will be more supportive of highs back in the upper 50s and low 60s 
across southern New England. Humidity also notably drops as drier 
air moves in, dropping dew points into the 40s and PWATs to 
generally around 0.25".

KEY MESSAGE 2...Fast-moving system expected to bring periods of rain 
Friday, followed by much colder and drier conditions Saturday.

High pressure today drifts off to the east and offshore later 
tonight ahead of a strong northern stream shortwave trough 
progressing east through the Great Lakes and into the northeast. 
Compared to last night's guidance, the timing for this front appears 
to have slowed down slightly, though this is still expected to be a 
quick moving system. The associated surface low is slated to track 
through the Great Lakes region, deepening as it moves northeast and 
reaching the 1000 mb mark (and possibly lower) by Friday morning, 
centered over southeast Ontario. Ensembles are in strong agreement 
with this threshold being crossed especially as it tracks into 
northern NY and VT by early Friday afternoon. Deterministic global 
guidance takes it to around 995 mb by the evening hours. Out ahead 
of the low, a warm front is expected to track into the region which 
will be the main driver for our first round of rain. Based on the 
latest guidance, rain is expected to move in closer to the 4-8 AM 
time range from west to east, spreading over the region. Once the 
warm front moves through, the warm sector settles in overhead. 925 
mb temperatures climb up again into the 16-18C range, especially in 
the afternoon, and anomalous PWATs increase up to around 1.75" with 
the moisture plume advected in by this system. Highs will be warmer 
than that of Thursday given this warm sector overhead during the day 
Friday, but not to the same level we saw Wednesday; highs will 
likely top out in the upper 60s with some places brushing 70. With 
the first round of rain out of the region by the afternoon, we're 
left with a muggy, breezy, and mild day. Some showers during this 
lull aren't out of the question, though, given the strong WAA.

Round two moves in toward the evening hours Friday ahead of the 
low's strong cold front. This front will provide strong forcing in 
an environment with bulk shear at 0-6 km expected to be at and above 
50 kt. A southerly LLJ sets up over much of eastern MA, RI, reaching 
40-50 kt at 925 mb and up to 60 kt over the region from the SW at 
850 mb. CAPE values top out around 500 J/kg based on the latest CAMs 
and global guidance, so while widespread severe weather is not 
expected, some embedded thunderstorms are not out of the question. 
With regards to rainfall totals, ensembles appear to have trended 
totals down slightly, generally ranging between 0.30"-0.60". 
Probabilities for totals reaching or exceeding an inch within 
southern New England have dropped considerably, though the GEFS does 
have a 20% chance across much of MA and into northern CT. Even with 
these low probabilities, the chance that there could be some 
convective features combined with these high PWAT values keeps the 
chance for some locally higher rainfall totals in play.

Breezy winds are expected for Friday given the aforementioned LLJ, 
though latest guidance has trended the intensity down slightly. This 
appears to be driven by the presence of a low-level thermal 
inversion noticeable in forecast soundings. Generally, gusts to 30 
mph seem most likely, though the waters may very well see gusts to 
the 35 mph range and higher given the warmer ocean temperatures. 

As the cold front crosses southern New England Saturday morning, 
strong CAA kicks off in its wake. 925 mb temperatures fall below 0C 
heading by Saturday evening, and PWATs fall below 0.25" once more as 
colder, drier air sets in. Lows Friday night fall into the 40s and 
upper 30s (towards the high elevations). Highs Saturday may struggle 
to reach the low 50s across the interior and lows Saturday night 
will likely dip below freezing across the region, with the 
exceptions being areas closest to the coasts and urban areas. 
Though, those areas will likely be sitting just above freezing 
overnight, with low 40s possible for the Cape and Islands. In the 
midst of this colder air, strong NW winds prevail, gusting well into 
the 30 mph range with some gusts to 40 mph not to be ruled out.
